The bourgeoisie (noun) refers to a social class — specifically, the class of people who own property, businesses, and capital, and who sit above the working class in society's economic hierarchy. Capital, simply put, is money or assets used to generate more money (through investment, ownership, or production).

The simplest picture: a factory owner, a wealthy merchant, a banker, a landlord — these are the kinds of people traditionally associated with the bourgeoisie. What unites them is not just that they are comfortable, but that they own the things that produce wealth, rather than simply working for someone else's wages.
The Two Main Ways the Word Is Used

The word operates meaningfully in two contexts, and you will encounter both.

In everyday, general usage, the bourgeoisie refers to the middle and upper-middle class — people who live comfortably, own property, have stable incomes, and tend to value respectability, social status, and material security. The word carries a mild flavour of conventionality and self-satisfaction in this sense. Someone described as "bourgeois" in this everyday way is typically seen as comfortable, conservative in taste, and preoccupied with appearances — the person with the nice house, the good job, the concern for what the neighbours think.

In its more precise, political and sociological usage — particularly in Marxist theory — the bourgeoisie has a sharper, more technical meaning. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels used it to describe the class that owns the means of production. The means of production is a key phrase: it refers to everything needed to produce goods and services — factories, machinery, land, raw materials, and capital. In other words, the bourgeoisie are not just "comfortable people." They are specifically the class of owners, whose wealth comes from owning these productive resources, not from the physical labour of their own hands.

Both usages are legitimate and widely used today. In academic, political, or economic discussions, the Marxist usage tends to dominate. In casual conversation, especially in European contexts, the everyday usage is more common.
What Makes Someone Part of the Bourgeoisie

The defining feature is ownership, not just wealth. A bourgeois person earns their living primarily through what they own — their business generates profit, their property generates rent, their investments generate returns. They do not (generally speaking) survive by selling their own physical labour by the hour. Their income flows from their position as owners.

They tend to hold values that protect and celebrate this ownership — belief in private property, individual initiative, rule of law, contracts, and the legitimacy of profit. Historically, they also sought political power that would reflect and protect these interests, which is why the rise of democracy and constitutional government in the 18th and 19th centuries is often closely linked with the rising power of the bourgeoisie.
How the Bourgeoisie Fits Into Society: The Class Picture

To fully understand the bourgeoisie, you need to understand who sits above and below them.

Below them: the proletariat. The proletariat (the working class) are those who own no significant property or capital. Their only economic resource is their own ability to work, so they sell their labour to the bourgeoisie for wages. The relationship between the two classes is central to Marxist thought: the bourgeoisie employ the proletariat, pay them wages, and retain the profit generated by their labour. Marx called this profit "surplus value" — the difference between what workers produce and what they are paid.

Above them historically: the aristocracy. Before the industrial and commercial revolutions reshaped Europe, the dominant class was the aristocracy — kings, nobles, and lords who inherited their status, titles, and land through bloodlines. The bourgeoisie were, for centuries, considered a lesser class because their wealth came from trade and commerce rather than noble birth, which was looked down upon by the old ruling elites. Over time, however, as capitalism expanded and industrial wealth became far more powerful than inherited land, the bourgeoisie displaced the aristocracy as the most influential class in society.

Within the bourgeoisie: the petit bourgeoisie. There is also a subdivision worth knowing — the petit bourgeoisie (or "petty bourgeoisie"), meaning the small bourgeoisie. This refers to people who own some means of production but on a modest scale — the small shopkeeper, the independent craftsperson, the self-employed professional, the small business owner who works alongside one or two employees. They are above the working class (they own something), but they are far removed from the major capitalist owners. They occupy a somewhat precarious, in-between social position.

Imagine a 19th-century English mill town. Mr. Ashworth owns the textile mill — the building, the looms, the raw cotton, and the finished product. He employs 300 men and women who come in each day, operate the machines, and receive a weekly wage in return. At the end of the month, Mr. Ashworth sells the cloth, pays his workers and other costs, and keeps the remaining profit. He lives in a large house, educates his children privately, attends church, and is deeply concerned with his family's standing in the community.

Mr. Ashworth is bourgeoisie. His 300 employees — who own nothing but their capacity to work and would starve without their wages — are the proletariat.

Now move this picture to the modern world. The owner of a chain of restaurants, a property developer who rents out dozens of apartments, a shareholder whose dividends fund their lifestyle — all of these fit the bourgeois profile in its essential structure, even if the context looks different.
The Connotations: How People Feel About This Word

Words carry attitudes, and "bourgeoisie" is no exception.

From a Marxist or left-wing perspective, the word is inherently critical. The bourgeoisie is seen as a class that maintains its wealth and power by exploiting the labour of the working class — and by controlling political, cultural, and legal institutions to keep this arrangement in place. In this view, what looks like a fair economic exchange (wages for work) is actually a form of systemic extraction that benefits the owners at the workers' expense.

From a neutral, sociological perspective, the word is purely descriptive — it names a class without passing judgment, the same way you might neutrally describe any other group.

In everyday or cultural conversation, it often implies a kind of comfortable, conventional, even slightly smug lifestyle — one that prioritises material security, social approval, and personal comfort over anything more radical or idealistic. To call someone's tastes or attitudes "bourgeois" in this sense is often a gentle (or not so gentle) criticism that they are unimaginative, conventional, and preoccupied with money and status.

The bourgeoisie is the social class defined by ownership — of capital, property, businesses, and the means of production. Their wealth comes from owning rather than labouring. They rose historically through trade and industry to replace the landed aristocracy as the dominant class in capitalist societies. In Marxist analysis, they stand in structural opposition to the proletariat, employing workers and retaining the profit of their labour. In broader cultural use, they represent comfortable, conventional, property-owning middle-class life — a lifestyle often associated with social respectability and material preoccupation.

Wherever you encounter this word — in political writing, in history books, in literature, in conversation — it is pointing at some version of this same core idea: the class of owners, the comfortable middle-to-upper class, defined by what they have rather than what they do with their hands.
